questions.stem: Canny edge detection uses two thresholds. What does the pair accomplish?
choices: One for horizontal and one for vertical edges
Hysteresis: pixels above the high threshold start an edge, and neighbouring pixels above the low threshold extend it, which keeps weak but connected edges while rejecting isolated noise
One for colour and one for grayscale
One for the gradient and one for the Laplacian
questions.explanation: A single threshold either fragments genuine edges or admits noise. Hysteresis seeds on confident pixels and grows along connected weaker ones, producing continuous contours. Canny also applies Gaussian smoothing and non-maximum suppression first, so the output is thin, connected edges.

questions.stem: What does non-maximum suppression do inside the Canny detector, as distinct from its role in object detection?
choices: It thins gradient ridges to single-pixel width by keeping only local maxima along the gradient direction
questions.explanation: The same name covers two different operations. In Canny, NMS thins a broad gradient response into a one-pixel ridge by keeping each pixel only if it is the maximum along the gradient normal. In detection, NMS removes overlapping boxes. Confusing the two is a common trap.

questions.stem: Why is a corner a better feature point than an edge for matching between images?
choices: An edge is ambiguous along its own direction, so its position cannot be localised in one dimension; a corner constrains both directions
questions.explanation: Sliding a window along an edge produces little change, so the match is undetermined in that direction — the aperture problem. At a corner, intensity changes in every direction, so the location is pinned in both axes. That is exactly what the Harris response measures.

questions.stem: Which TWO properties should a good local descriptor have for matching across viewpoints?
choices: Invariance to rotation and scale, so the same physical point matches despite camera motion
Distinctiveness, so different points produce clearly different descriptors
questions.explanation: Invariance ensures the same point is described the same way from a different viewpoint; distinctiveness ensures different points are not confused. Brightness dependence destroys invariance under lighting change, which is why descriptors normalise. Longer vectors cost memory and match time without inherently helping.

questions.stem: What problem does RANSAC solve when estimating a homography from matched keypoints?
choices: Correspondences contain gross outliers, and least squares is destroyed by them; RANSAC fits from random minimal subsets and keeps the model with most inliers
It converts the homography to affine
questions.explanation: Feature matching always produces some completely wrong pairs, and a single bad correspondence can wreck a least-squares fit. RANSAC repeatedly samples the minimum number of points, scores each candidate by inlier count, and returns the consensus model. It is robust precisely because it never averages outliers in.

questions.stem: What do a camera's intrinsic parameters describe?
choices: Its position and orientation in the world
Focal length, principal point and skew — the mapping from camera coordinates to pixel coordinates
questions.explanation: Intrinsics are properties of the camera and lens: how 3D points in the camera frame project onto the sensor grid. Extrinsics describe where the camera sits in the world. Calibration estimates intrinsics and distortion coefficients, usually from images of a known pattern.

questions.stem: Straight lines in your images bow outward near the edges. What is this and how is it corrected?
choices: Motion blur; use a faster shutter
Radial lens distortion; estimate distortion coefficients by calibration and undistort the image or the point coordinates
questions.explanation: Barrel distortion is radial: displacement grows with distance from the optical centre. Calibration with a chessboard or circle grid estimates the coefficients, after which images can be remapped or measurements corrected analytically. Any geometric measurement on a wide-angle lens is wrong until this is handled.

questions.stem: In a calibrated stereo pair, what does the disparity of a matched point tell you?
choices: Its depth: disparity is inversely proportional to distance, scaled by the baseline and focal length
questions.explanation: Depth equals focal length times baseline divided by disparity. Near points shift a lot between the two views and far points barely at all, which is also why stereo range accuracy degrades quadratically with distance and why a wider baseline improves far-field depth.

questions.stem: Why is rectification performed before stereo matching?
choices: To warp both images so corresponding points lie on the same horizontal row, reducing the search for a match from two dimensions to one
To crop to the overlapping region
questions.explanation: Epipolar geometry already constrains a match to a line; rectification aligns those lines with image rows. The search then becomes a 1D scan along a row, which is both far faster and far more robust than an unconstrained 2D search.

questions.stem: Which TWO situations still favour classical computer vision over a learned model?
choices: A fixed industrial setup with controlled lighting where a geometric measurement must be exact and explainable
Very little or no labelled data, with the target defined by precise geometry or colour rather than appearance variation
Recognising thousands of object categories in unconstrained photographs
questions.explanation: Classical methods win where the problem is geometric, the environment is controlled, and the answer must be deterministic and auditable — calibration, fiducial markers, metrology. Open-world appearance variation is where learned features are indispensable.

questions.stem: What does template matching fundamentally struggle with?
choices: Changes in scale, rotation and illumination, because it slides a fixed patch and compares pixels directly
questions.explanation: Template matching correlates a fixed patch across the image, so any transformation the template does not itself contain breaks the match. It works well for a rigid, known appearance at known scale — a UI element, a printed mark — and fails as soon as viewpoint varies.

questions.stem: What does the Hough transform do for line detection?
choices: Maps each edge pixel to a curve in parameter space and finds lines as accumulator peaks, which tolerates gaps and occlusion
Fits a single line by least squares
questions.explanation: Because every edge pixel votes for all lines passing through it, a line appears as a peak where many pixels agree. That voting scheme makes it robust to broken and partially occluded lines, unlike a fit that needs contiguous support.

questions.stem: You need sub-pixel accuracy locating a calibration target's corners. What is the standard approach?
choices: Upscale the image 4x and detect again
Detect corners at pixel level, then refine iteratively using the local gradient structure, since the true corner rarely sits at a pixel centre
questions.explanation: Integer pixel positions cap accuracy at roughly half a pixel, which is not enough for calibration. Refinement exploits the fact that gradient vectors near a corner are orthogonal to the displacement toward it, solving for the sub-pixel location. Upscaling invents no new information.

questions.stem: Why does contour area alone poorly distinguish object classes in a binary image?
choices: Objects of different shapes can share an area, so shape descriptors such as aspect ratio, solidity, extent or Hu moments are needed to separate them
questions.explanation: Area is a single scalar and collapses all shape information. A circle and a thin rectangle can have identical area. Combining area with ratios that capture elongation and convexity gives a descriptor that actually discriminates, which is the basis of classical blob classification.

questions.stem: Feature matching between two views yields many matches but the homography is wrong. Inlier count is low. What should you check first?
choices: Whether the scene is actually planar or the camera only rotated — a homography is valid for a plane or for pure rotation, and fails on a general 3D scene with translation
Whether the images are the same size
questions.explanation: A homography is not a general scene model. It holds for a planar surface, or for any scene when the camera rotates about its optical centre without translating. Photographing a 3D scene from two positions produces parallax that no homography can explain, so inliers stay low however good the matches are.
